picks.title: A Google-like search engine for single-cell RNA data could answer previously impossible questions
picks.excerpt: Max Delbruck Center researchers built Malva, a search platform that queries millions of single cells using raw sequence information alone, finding RNA isoforms and rare variants without reference genomes or huge downloads. The team frames it as infrastructure that both scientists and AI tools can query in seconds.
picks.rationale: Turns single-cell biology's dataset problem into a search problem, and is explicitly built so AI agents can query it — new research infrastructure, not a rehash.

picks.title: Researchers develop AI framework to optimize solid oxide electrolysis cell operation
picks.excerpt: A Seoul National University of Science and Technology team replaced 6,561 simulations with 17, using an AI-guided search that improved electrochemical performance 14% and cut temperature gradients by 80% in solid oxide electrolysis cells.
picks.rationale: 6,561 simulations down to 17 with 14% better performance — the most concretely quantified collapse of a design-search budget in the pool.

picks.title: Going beyond simple models of neural networks: Extended mean-field theory offers a better approach
picks.excerpt: Princeton physicists found that standard mean-field theory fails to reproduce real neuron activity, but an extended version that carries full probability distributions matched recordings from over 1,000 mouse brain neurons.
picks.rationale: A theory upgrade validated against 1,000+ real neurons that changes how both brains and artificial networks get modeled — physics and neuroscience in one result.

picks.title: FAU Researchers Use Quantum Machine Learning to Predict Heart Disease
picks.excerpt: Florida Atlantic University researchers benchmarked quantum feature maps and quantum classifiers on clinical data from 918 patients, reporting 90.26% accuracy for heart disease prediction and mapping where quantum encoding helps versus classical baselines.
picks.rationale: Quantum machine learning measured on a real 918-patient clinical dataset instead of a toy benchmark — a rare concrete data point on where QML actually helps.

picks.title: AI doesn't just play better chess - it manages complexity differently
picks.excerpt: Complexity Science Hub and University of Parma researchers analyzed over 2,000 games and found engines sustain high board complexity far longer than humans, who simplify positions early even when their peak tension matches the machine's.
picks.rationale: Quantifies a real cognitive split between human and machine problem-solving — humans bail out of complexity early, engines hold it — using a measurable proxy across 2,000+ games.
